title: Be slow to judge (Avot 1:1)
hookLine: the Great Assembly: be deliberate in judgment, raise many students, build a fence round the Torah

cards: It takes about a second. A screenshot, a headline, a neighbor's car parked badly, a coworker's short email. And the verdict is in.
Clueless. People judge faster than they breathe, and the internet has made it a sport. Now picture a council of sages, the Great Assembly, at the end of that long chain from Sinai.
They've been handed everything. And when Avot finally gives them a voice, the very first advice they pass on is about speed.

teach.b: The men of the Great Assembly, Avot says, said three things. Be deliberate in judgment. Raise up many students.
And make a fence around the Torah. The first one holds today's word. In Hebrew, hevu metunim ba-din.

Metunim means slow, measured, patient: the slowness of someone who takes a second look. They were speaking first to judges, the people who decide real cases, and Jewish law built that slowness into its courts.
The Mishnah says that in a capital case, the old high court could acquit a person on the same day, but could not convict on the same day.
A guilty verdict had to wait until tomorrow, so the judges would sleep on it and look for any merit they'd missed. Mercy could be quick. Condemnation had to be slow.
The other two sayings fit around this one.
Raise up many students: don't hoard what you know. One old story says the school of Shammai wanted to teach only the worthy, and the school of Hillel said teach everyone.
Make a fence around the Torah: a little margin of care, so you don't stumble over the line itself. But the order matters.
Before students, before fences: slow down. Few people sit on a court, but everyone judges all day long. Kids, partners, strangers on a train.
The sages' first advice: whatever verdict you're about to reach, let it wait a moment longer.

how: Jewish law sets out careful procedures for courts, including questioning witnesses closely and, in capital cases, delaying any guilty verdict until the next day, and Avot's call to judge deliberately is often applied to everyday life.

o: wise and learned, knowing the whole law
measured and patient, slow to reach a verdict
strict and stern, never showing any mercy

games.q: three things the Assembly said — tap the pairs.
p: a margin of care around the line
had to wait until the next day

s: the old high court could convict and acquit on the same day
it could acquit the same day, but a guilty verdict in a capital case had to wait until tomorrow.
hevu metunim ba-din: be deliberate in judgment.
the Great Assembly's advice was only for judges
it was said first to judges, and has been applied to everyday judging ever since.

games.q: you're a judge on the old high court. the evidence in a capital case points to guilty, and it's late afternoon. what does the law say?
o: wait until tomorrow before a guilty verdict.
games.why: the Mishnah says an acquittal could come the same day, but a conviction had to wait until the next day, so judges could look again for merit.

practice: Think of a verdict you reached recently, fast, about a coworker, a relative, a stranger, someone online, and put it on hold, like the old court. Ask what you might not know, and what a good lawyer for this person would say.
You don't have to change your mind; just let the verdict wait until tomorrow.

wordCard.voice: Metunim. Measured, patient, slow to decide: the word behind the Great Assembly's first saying in Avot, be deliberate in judgment.
